newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian OLOs caught between U.S. bears, Euro bulls.
newsitem.headline: Belgian OLOs caught between U.S. bears, Euro bulls.

text.p: Scrambling for direction, the Belgian government bond (OLO) market is trapped between bears pointing to a likely cycle of U.S. interest rate rises and bulls flagging positive trends in Europe, dealers said on Wednesday.
The net outcome of the tussle is likely to be a stalemate for now, leaving players sitting on their hands and dealers marking prices down to attract business in a thin market.

"It is all a question of how far you want to look ahead," a trader said. Fresh clues as to the course of U.S. rate policy will come on Friday afternoon in the shape of retail sales and factory gate price data for March US-ECI.

Growth of U.S. retail sales is seen easing off, while PPIs are expected to show slower growth year-on-year. If in line with the forecasts, both sets of numbers would be bond-positive, but that does not imply markets will rally, dealers said.
"The U.S. market has a distinct bear tone to it," one said. "It is marked by fears for a rate hike."

Another bear said gains on the European markets at the start of the week in the wake of fresh optimism economic and monetary union (EMU) would go ahead as planned and the Maastricht Treaty criteria would be applied strictly had been overdone. "Europe has outperformed the U.S. by quite a lot," he said.
"It is better to be careful at these levels," he added.

One analyst said that while lower U.S. Treasuries and a pick-up in the German economy might in the next three months push the yield on the benchmark 10-year Bund up to 6.50 percent from about 5.90 percent on Wednesday.

With Germany being Belgium's main export partner, Belgian rates are tied closely to German ones. The Belgian 10-year benchmark yield was steady at 6.03 percent at 0910 GMT, but down from levels at around 6.10 percent this time last week.

But looking ahead, the analyst said, the back-up in German rates would be limited in view of the currently low inflation, modest wage increases with the upside scope limited by a lax labour market, and a likely slowdown in U.S. growth.
This meant German rates and yields, and consequently Belgian rates and yields, would not rise much further than 6.50 percent, she added.
